```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(here)
library(recipes) 
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)
library(broom)

# Same colours as workspace.Rmd
blue   <- "#2a78d6"
orange <- "#eb6834"
grey   <- "#d8d8d4"
red    <- "#e34948"

# Settings you might want to change later
MIN_EST <- 10   # keep combos averaging at least this many establishments per year

# Helper to save every plot into plots/clustering/
dir.create(here("plots", "clustering"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
save_plot <- function(p, name, w = 9, h = 6) {
  ggsave(here("plots", "clustering", paste0(name, ".png")),
         plot = p, width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
}
```

```{r load-data}
rds_path <- here("data", "df_small_clean.rds")

if (file.exists(rds_path)) {
  df_small_clean <- readRDS(rds_path)
} else {
  # Fallback: rebuild only what we need straight from the CSV
  df_small_clean <- read.csv(here("business-establishments-and-jobs-data-by-business-size-and-anzsic.csv")) |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    rename(total_active_establishments = total_establishments)
}

# census_year is a Date in workspace.Rmd; turn it back into a plain number (2002, 2003, ...)
df <- df_small_clean |>
  mutate(year = if (inherits(census_year, "Date")) as.integer(format(census_year, "%Y"))
                else as.integer(census_year)) |>
  select(year, clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, business_size, total_active_establishments)

# Quick sanity checks
range(df$year)                    # expect 2002 2024
n_distinct(df$clue_small_area)    # expect 13
n_distinct(df$anzsic_indusrty)    # expect 19
```

# 1. Build the panel (one row per area x industry x year)

This adds up the business sizes, so we get one count per combo per year. Then it
**fills in the missing zeros** (the CSV leaves out rows where a combo had 0 businesses).

```{r panel}
panel <- df |>
  group_by(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, year) |>
  summarise(est = sum(total_active_establishments), .groups = "drop") |>
  complete(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, year = 2002:2024,
           fill = list(est = 0))

# Every combo should now have all 23 years: 13 areas x 19 industries x 23 years
stopifnot(nrow(panel) == 13 * 19 * 23)

# How many zeros did we just fill in?
sum(panel$est == 0)

# Citywide total per year: should match the blue line in interim Figure 2
panel |> group_by(year) |> summarise(city_total = sum(est)) |> print(n = 23)
```

**Check:** 5,681 rows; the yearly totals start at 12,139 (2002) and end at 14,338 (2024).
If the totals don't match Figure 2, something went wrong in loading.

**Understand:** without `complete()`, a combo missing 2011 would silently jump from 2010
to 2012 in any growth calculation.

We also keep the business-size breakdown on the side. It is **not** a clustering input;
we use it in Step 8 to describe the clusters.

```{r size-mix}
size_mix <- df |>
  group_by(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, business_size) |>
  summarise(est = sum(total_active_establishments), .groups = "drop")
```

# 2. Build the three "report card" numbers per combo

Each combo gets one growth number per window. The three windows are 2002–18 (long run,
before COVID), 2018–22 (COVID) and 2022–24 (recovery). We use the **annualised log change**:

`(log(end + 1) - log(start + 1)) / number_of_years`

The `+ 1` stops log(0) from breaking, and logs calm down silly jumps like 2 → 6.
Roughly, 0.05 ≈ +5% per year, and -0.05 ≈ -5% per year.

**Why these windows:** the interim showed the conclusion flips depending on the period
compared, so we need several. The GFC boundaries (2008, 2012) were dropped after a dip test
in 2b below (7 of 19 industries dipped, against a pre-set threshold of 10; COVID: 15 of 19).

```{r features}
ann_log_change <- function(from, to, n_years) (log(to + 1) - log(from + 1)) / n_years

features_all <- panel |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = est, names_prefix = "y") |>
  mutate(
    combo      = paste0(anzsic_indusrty, " | ", clue_small_area),
    mean_est   = rowMeans(pick(starts_with("y"))),
    g_long     = ann_log_change(y2002, y2018, 16),  # long run, before COVID
    g_covid    = ann_log_change(y2018, y2022, 4),   # COVID
    g_recovery = ann_log_change(y2022, y2024, 2)    # recovery
  )

feature_cols   <- c("g_long", "g_covid", "g_recovery")

# Nice labels for plots later
feature_labels <- c(g_long     = "Long run\n2002–18",
                    g_covid    = "COVID\n2018–22",
                    g_recovery = "Recovery\n2022–24")
```

**Understand:** the three windows add up to the whole 2002–2024 period, so we don't also
need a separate "overall growth" feature (it would just double-count).

**Known limitations to mention in the report:**

- Each window uses single endpoint years. Some areas repeat the previous year's values
  (not surveyed every year), so an endpoint can be slightly stale. This matters most for
  the 2-year recovery window, where one stale endpoint is a large share of the period.
- A per-year growth rate is a looser summary of a 16-year window than of a 2-year window,
  and the short-window rates are the noisiest.

# 2b. Is the GFC window a real shock?

A shock should show up as a dip: growth over 2008-12 lower than the windows either side.
COVID (2018-22 vs 2012-18 and 2022-24) is the benchmark for what a real shock looks like.
With three noisy windows, the middle one is lowest ~1 time in 3 by chance (~6 of 19 industries).

**Threshold, set before running:** the GFC window counts as a shock if >= 10 of 19 industries dip.

```{r gfc-dip-test}
GFC_THRESHOLD <- 10

ind_year <- panel |>
  group_by(anzsic_indusrty, year) |>
  summarise(est = sum(est), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = est, names_prefix = "y")

dip_test <- ind_year |>
  mutate(g_0208 = ann_log_change(y2002, y2008, 6),
         g_0812 = ann_log_change(y2008, y2012, 4),
         g_1218 = ann_log_change(y2012, y2018, 6),
         g_1822 = ann_log_change(y2018, y2022, 4),
         g_2224 = ann_log_change(y2022, y2024, 2),
         gfc_dip   = g_0812 < g_0208 & g_0812 < g_1218,
         covid_dip = g_1822 < g_1218 & g_1822 < g_2224) |>
  select(anzsic_indusrty, starts_with("g_"), gfc_dip, covid_dip)

# Growth shown as % per year
dip_test |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("g_"), \(g) round((exp(g) - 1) * 100, 1))) |>
  arrange(anzsic_indusrty)

tibble(window   = c("GFC 2008-12", "COVID 2018-22", "Chance (approx.)"),
       dips     = c(sum(dip_test$gfc_dip), sum(dip_test$covid_dip), round(19 / 3)),
       of       = 19)

# TRUE = GFC is a real shock (keep its boundaries); FALSE = drop them
sum(dip_test$gfc_dip) >= GFC_THRESHOLD
```

**Result:** GFC dips in 7/19 industries (chance ~6), COVID in 15/19, so the line above prints
`FALSE`. The GFC window fails the pre-set threshold and the 2008 and 2012 boundaries are
dropped. City-wide establishments kept rising through 2008-12 (15,364 -> 16,091); growth
slowed rather than dipped.

**Caveat:** carried-forward survey years could flatten a real dip.

# 3. Drop the tiny combos

```{r filter}
features <- features_all |> filter(mean_est >= MIN_EST)

# How many combos do we keep, and what share of all establishments do they cover?
tibble(
  combos_total   = sum(features_all$mean_est > 0),
  combos_kept    = nrow(features),
  pct_est_kept   = sum(features$mean_est) / sum(features_all$mean_est) * 100
)

# Which industries lose the most combos? (tells you where coverage is thin)
features_all |>
  filter(mean_est > 0) |>
  mutate(kept = mean_est >= MIN_EST) |>
  count(anzsic_indusrty, kept) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = kept, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  rename(dropped = `FALSE`, kept = `TRUE`) |>
  arrange(desc(dropped))
```

**Check:** you keep roughly 150 combos but still cover almost all establishments
(tiny combos are many but small). Industries like Mining and Agriculture will lose most
of their combos; say so in the report ("too small to cluster reliably").

**Check (replication):** the three-window rebuild should reproduce the earlier combo counts,
because `MIN_EST` uses each combo's average across all years, not the windows. Expect 153
combos covering 97.7% of establishments, and city totals of 12,139 (2002), 16,768 (2018),
13,828 (2022) and 14,338 (2024). The last line counts kept combos with a zero at a window
endpoint, which is where `log(x + 1)` would differ from `log(x)`.

```{r replication-check}
nrow(features)                                              
sum(features$mean_est) / sum(features_all$mean_est) * 100   

panel |> group_by(year) |> summarise(city_total = sum(est)) |>
  filter(year %in% c(2002, 2018, 2022, 2024))               

sum(apply(features[, c("y2002", "y2018", "y2022", "y2024")] == 0, 1, any))
```

**Try later:** set `MIN_EST <- 5` at the top and re-run. If the clusters tell the same
story, write "results were robust to the size threshold".

# 3b. Rule-based classification (primary method)

Each combo is labelled with one of five classes, using the direction of growth in each of
the three windows. A window is **+** if growth is above +1% a year, **-** if below -1% a year,
and **flat** otherwise. **Recovered** means the total gain over 2022-24 is at least the total
loss over 2018-22; in log rates, 2 x g_recovery >= -4 x g_covid.

**Where the classes come from:** the research question (declining / recovering / growing) and
the interim's three stories (existing decline, temporary setback, incomplete recovery).

| Class | Source |
|---|---|
| Stable or growing | RQ: "growing" |
| Covid setback, Recovered | Interim: "temporary setback" |
| Covid setback, Recovering | Interim: "incomplete recovery"; RQ: "recovering" |
| Covid setback, No recovery yet | RQ: "declining", applied after the COVID shock |
| Long-run decline | Interim: "existing decline" |

**Revised after a first run (state this in the report).** A first version used five predefined
stories as written. 82 of 153 combos (54%) fit none of them, above the pre-set limit of 10%.
The main gap was combos still falling after COVID, so that class was added and the others
widened to cover every pattern. No combo is left unlabelled.

**Rules, checked in order (a combo takes the first class it matches):**

| Order | Class | Rule (2002-18, 2018-22, 2022-24) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Long-run decline | 2002-18 is - (any COVID, any recovery) |
| 2 | Covid setback, Recovered | 2018-22 is -, 2022-24 is +, recovered |
| 3 | Covid setback, Recovering | 2018-22 is -, 2022-24 is +, not recovered |
| 4 | Covid setback, No recovery yet | 2018-22 is - and 2022-24 is - or flat; or + / flat / - |
| 5 | Stable or growing | everything else (long run not -, no fall in 2018-22) |

**Notes for the report:**

- Long-run decline includes combos that are rebounding since 2022 (pattern - / any / +).
- Judgement call: + / flat / - (grew in the long run, flat through COVID, falling since) is
  placed in "Declining since COVID".
- "Stable or growing" includes some combos that are flat, or slightly falling since 2022,
  but were not knocked down by COVID.

**Set before running:** flat band +/-1% a year. Sensitivity: re-label with bands of +/-0.5% and
+/-1.5%. If more than `SENS_MAX` of combos change class at either band, the labels are
reported as fragile.

```{r rules}
FLAT_BAND  <- 1            # % per year
SENS_BANDS <- c(0.5, 1.5)  # % per year
SENS_MAX   <- 0.20         # CONFIRM BEFORE RUNNING: labels are fragile if more than this share changes

class_levels <- c("Stable or growing", "Covid setback, Recovered", "Covid setback, Recovering",
                  "Covid setback, No recovery yet", "Long-run decline")

# Direction of one window: "+", "-" or "0" (flat), judged on % change per year
direction <- function(g, band = FLAT_BAND) {
  pct <- (exp(g) - 1) * 100
  case_when(pct > band ~ "+", pct < -band ~ "-", TRUE ~ "0")
}

# Reusable for the grants track: give it the three window growth rates.
# case_when takes the first rule that matches, so the order matters.
classify_story <- function(g_long, g_covid, g_recovery, band = FLAT_BAND) {
  L <- direction(g_long, band); C <- direction(g_covid, band); R <- direction(g_recovery, band)
  recovered <- 2 * g_recovery >= -4 * g_covid   # window lengths: 2 and 4 years
  out <- case_when(
    L == "-"                           ~ "Long-run decline",
    C == "-" & R == "+" &  recovered   ~ "Covid setback, Recovered",
    C == "-" & R == "+" & !recovered   ~ "Covid setback, Recovering",
    C == "-"                           ~ "Covid setback, No recovery yet",
    L == "+" & C == "0" & R == "-"     ~ "Covid setback, No recovery yet",   # judgement call
    TRUE                               ~ "Stable or growing"
  )
  factor(out, levels = class_levels)
}

features <- features |>
  mutate(story   = classify_story(g_long, g_covid, g_recovery),
         pattern = paste0(direction(g_long), direction(g_covid), direction(g_recovery)))

stopifnot(!any(is.na(features$story)))   # every combo gets a class

# How many combos, and what share of establishments, in each class?
features |>
  group_by(story, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarise(n_combos = n(), est = sum(mean_est), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct_combos = round(n_combos / sum(n_combos) * 100, 1),
         pct_est    = round(est / sum(est) * 100, 1))

# Which patterns make up each class? (long run, COVID, recovery)
features |> count(story, pattern) |> arrange(story, desc(n))

to_pct <- function(g) (exp(g) - 1) * 100

severity <- features |>
  group_by(story) |>
  summarise(
    n_combos          = n(),
    covid_median      = round(to_pct(median(g_covid)), 1),     # % per year, 2018-22
    covid_worst       = round(to_pct(min(g_covid)), 1),
    covid_mildest     = round(to_pct(max(g_covid)), 1),
    recovery_median   = round(to_pct(median(g_recovery)), 1),  # % per year, 2022-24
    pct_vs_2018       = round((sum(y2024) / sum(y2018) - 1) * 100, 1),
    est_change_18_24  = sum(y2024) - sum(y2018),
    .groups = "drop")
severity

p_severity <- features |>
  mutate(covid = to_pct(g_covid), recovery = to_pct(g_recovery)) |>
  ggplot(aes(covid, recovery, colour = story, size = mean_est)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = class_cols) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "COVID fall vs recovery, by class",
       subtitle = "One dot per combo; size = average establishments per year",
       x = "Growth 2018–22 (% per year)", y = "Growth 2022–24 (% per year)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_severity
save_plot(p_severity, "19_severity_scatter", w = 10, h = 7)
```

```{r rules-sensitivity}
# Labels under each band
map_dfr(c(SENS_BANDS[1], FLAT_BAND, SENS_BANDS[2]), \(b)
  tibble(band  = b,
         story = classify_story(features$g_long, features$g_covid, features$g_recovery, b))) |>
  count(band, story, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = band, values_from = n, names_prefix = "band_")

# How many combos change class compared with +/-1%, and is that above SENS_MAX?
sens <- map_dfr(SENS_BANDS, \(b) tibble(
  band    = b,
  changed = sum(classify_story(features$g_long, features$g_covid, features$g_recovery, b) !=
                features$story)))
sens |> mutate(pct_changed = round(changed / nrow(features) * 100, 1),
               fragile     = changed / nrow(features) > SENS_MAX)

# Largest combos per class, with 2018 / 2022 / 2024 counts
features |> group_by(story) |> slice_max(mean_est, n = 3) |>
  select(story, combo, y2018, y2022, y2024)

# Share of each industry's and each area's establishments in each class
class_share <- function(by) features |>
  group_by({{ by }}, story, .drop = FALSE) |> summarise(est = sum(mean_est), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by({{ by }}) |> mutate(pct = round(est / sum(est) * 100)) |> select(-est) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = story, values_from = pct)
class_share(anzsic_indusrty)
class_share(clue_small_area)

# Classification plots
class_cols <- c("Stable or growing"              = blue,
                "Covid setback, Recovered"       = "#9cc3f0",
                "Covid setback, Recovering"      = "#f5b08f",
                "Covid setback, No recovery yet" = orange,
                "Long-run decline"               = "#7a1a1a")

plot_class_share <- function(by, title, caption = NULL) {
  dat <- features |>
    group_by(unit = {{ by }}) |>
    mutate(unit = paste0(unit, " (", n(), ")")) |>          # (n) = number of combos
    group_by(unit, story) |>
    summarise(est = sum(mean_est), .groups = "drop") |>
    group_by(unit) |>
    mutate(share    = est / sum(est),
           not_back = sum(share[story %in% c("Covid setback, No recovery yet",
                                             "Long-run decline")])) |>
    ungroup()

  ggplot(dat, aes(share, fct_reorder(unit, not_back), fill = story)) +
    geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = class_cols, drop = FALSE) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = "Share of establishments (average per year); (n) = number of combos",
         caption = caption, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

p_class_ind <- plot_class_share(anzsic_indusrty, "Classification by industry",
  caption = "Agriculture not shown: no combo averages 10+ establishments a year. Mining = CBD only.")
p_class_ind
save_plot(p_class_ind, "17_class_by_industry", w = 12, h = 7)

p_class_area <- plot_class_share(clue_small_area, "Classification by area")
p_class_area
save_plot(p_class_area, "18_class_by_area", w = 12, h = 7)
```

**Result:** 
at ±1%, 28 combos are stable or growing, 13 are Covid setback, Recovered, 34 are Covid setback, Recovering, 44 are Covid setback, No recovery yet, and 34 are in long-run decline. The three Covid setback classes cover 91 combos and about 78% of establishments. The labels are not fragile: 9 combos (5.9%) change class at ±0.5% and 11 (7.2%) at ±1.5%, below the pre-set 20% threshold. Long-run decline is the most sensitive class (38 combos at ±0.5%, 26 at ±1.5%), because many 16-year growth rates sit close to ±1% a year.

# 4. Look at the features before clustering

```{r explore-hist, fig.height = 4}
p_feat_hist <- features |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(feature_cols), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature_labels[feature], levels = feature_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = blue) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of annualised growth in each window",
       x = "Annualised log change (0.05 ≈ +5%/yr)", y = "Number of combos") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_feat_hist
save_plot(p_feat_hist, "01_feature_histograms", w = 11, h = 4)
```

**Check:** the COVID window should sit mostly left of zero. The 2-year recovery window is
expected to be the most spread out (shortest window, so the noisiest). The windows have
different centres and spreads, which is exactly why we standardise in Step 5.

```{r explore-corr, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
corr_long <- cor(features[, feature_cols]) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r")

p_corr <- ggplot(corr_long, aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = red, mid = "white", high = blue, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between the three growth windows", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_corr
save_plot(p_corr, "02_feature_correlation", w = 6, h = 5)
```

**Check:** no pair should be above about 0.8. If two windows were that correlated they
would be saying the same thing twice. Negative correlations between neighbouring windows
are normal (a big boom is often followed by a fall back).

```{r explore-outliers}
# Combos that are extreme (more than 3 SDs from the mean) in any window
features |>
  mutate(across(all_of(feature_cols), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)), .names = "z_{.col}")) |>
  filter(if_any(starts_with("z_"), ~ abs(.x) > 3)) |>
  select(combo, mean_est, y2002, y2018, y2022, y2024, all_of(feature_cols)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_est))
```

**Check:** previously Docklands combos showed up here (it started from almost nothing in 2002);
confirm whether that still holds on the three windows.
k-means is sensitive to outliers, so note which combos these are. If one of them ends up
alone in its own cluster, that is a sign it's an outlier, not a real segment.

# 5. Standardise

```{r standardise}
rec <- recipe(~ ., data = features |> select(all_of(feature_cols))) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

clust_data <- prep(rec) |> bake(new_data = NULL)

# Verify: every mean ≈ 0, every SD = 1
clust_data |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(value), 4), sd = sd(value))
```

# 6. How many clusters? (elbow, silhouette, gap)

No sampling needed like in GA_2: we only have ~150 rows.

**Re-check needed:** "diagnostics inconclusive" was concluded on the old five-window features.
Re-read the three plots below and record whether it still holds. This is the evidence for using
rule-based classification as the primary method and clustering as a check.

```{r diag-elbow, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
set.seed(123)
p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(clust_data, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 10, nstart = 50)
p_elbow
save_plot(p_elbow, "03_elbow", w = 7, h = 4.5)
```

```{r diag-silhouette, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
set.seed(123)
p_sil <- fviz_nbclust(clust_data, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 10, nstart = 50)
p_sil
save_plot(p_sil, "04_silhouette", w = 7, h = 4.5)
```

```{r diag-gap, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
set.seed(123)
p_gap <- fviz_nbclust(clust_data, kmeans, method = "gap_stat", k.max = 10,
                      nstart = 25, iter.max = 50, nboot = 100)
p_gap
save_plot(p_gap, "05_gap", w = 7, h = 4.5)
```

**Understand:**

- **Elbow:** where adding another cluster stops helping much.
- **Silhouette:** how clearly each combo belongs to its cluster. Above ~0.25 is "some
  real structure"; above ~0.5 is strong. Don't expect strong with real economic data.
- **Gap:** whether the clusters are better than what random data would give.

They will probably disagree. Pick a k in the range they point to that gives clusters you
can explain, and **write down why** in the report.

# 7. Fit k-means and check it's stable

```{r choose-k}
K <- 5 # one cluster per rule-based class
```

```{r fit}
set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(clust_data, centers = K, nstart = 50, iter.max = 50)

# k-means numbers clusters randomly. Re-number them so cluster 1 = weakest overall
# growth and cluster K = strongest. This keeps labels the same every time you re-run.
# Overall growth = total log change over 2002-24: each window's rate times its length in years.
window_years   <- c(16, 4, 2)   # same order as feature_cols
overall_growth <- as.vector(as.matrix(features[, feature_cols]) %*% window_years)
cluster_order  <- tapply(overall_growth, km$cluster, mean) |> rank()
cluster_vec    <- as.integer(cluster_order[as.character(km$cluster)])

table(cluster_vec)
```

**Check:** no cluster should have only 1–3 combos. If one does, it's probably an outlier
from Step 4; try a smaller K or note it as a special case.

```{r silhouette-fit, fig.height = 5}
sil <- silhouette(cluster_vec, dist(clust_data))
summary(sil)$clus.avg.widths   # average silhouette per cluster
p_sil_fit <- fviz_silhouette(sil, print.summary = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Silhouette for k = ", K)) +
  theme_minimal()
p_sil_fit
save_plot(p_sil_fit, "06_silhouette_fit")
```



**Understand:** each bar is one combo. Bars below zero are combos that sit closer to a
different cluster than their own ("fence-sitters"). A few are normal; lots of them in one
cluster means that cluster is weak.

```{r stability}
# (a) Different random seeds: do we get the same clusters?
ari_seeds <- map_dbl(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster_vec, kmeans(clust_data, K, nstart = 50)$cluster)
})

# (b) Bootstrap: refit on a random 80% of combos, compare on the combos they share
ari_boot <- map_dbl(1:100, function(b) {
  set.seed(1000 + b)
  idx <- sample(nrow(clust_data), floor(0.8 * nrow(clust_data)))
  fit <- kmeans(clust_data[idx, ], K, nstart = 25)
  mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster_vec[idx], fit$cluster)
})

# (c) PAM: a more outlier-resistant cousin of k-means. Does it agree?
pam_fit <- pam(clust_data, K)
ari_pam <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster_vec, pam_fit$clustering)

tibble(
  check = c("Different seeds (median ARI)", "Bootstrap 80% (median ARI)",
            "Bootstrap 80% (worst 10% ARI)", "k-means vs PAM (ARI)"),
  value = round(c(median(ari_seeds), median(ari_boot),
                  quantile(ari_boot, 0.1), ari_pam), 2)
)

table(kmeans = cluster_vec, pam = pam_fit$clustering)
```

**Understand ARI (adjusted Rand index):** 1 = identical clusters, 0 = no better than random.
Rough guide: above 0.8 very stable, 0.6–0.8 reasonably stable, below 0.5 shaky.

**Check:** seeds should be ~1 (nstart = 50 makes this easy). The bootstrap is the real test.
In the PAM table, each k-means cluster should mostly map onto one PAM cluster (the column
order may differ, that's fine).

## 7b. Do the clusters line up with the rule-based classes?

Clustering is a check on the rules, not a replacement. For each class, we look at how its
combos spread across clusters, and at overall agreement (ARI). K = 5 is the direct test
(one cluster per class); K = 3 and 4 are secondary. No threshold is set: the results are
described, not labelled as "supported" or "not supported".

```{r compare-rules}
to_pct <- function(g) (exp(g) - 1) * 100

compare_k <- function(k) {
  set.seed(123)   # same settings as the main fit, so K = 5 reproduces it
  cl  <- kmeans(clust_data, centers = k, nstart = 50, iter.max = 50)$cluster
  tab <- table(class = features$story, cluster = cl)
  list(
    counts    = tab,
    row_pct   = round(prop.table(tab, 1) * 100),          # % of each class in each cluster
    top_share = tibble(class           = rownames(tab),
                       n               = as.vector(rowSums(tab)),
                       top_cluster     = colnames(tab)[apply(tab, 1, which.max)],
                       top_cluster_pct = round(apply(tab, 1, max) / rowSums(tab) * 100)),
    profile   = features |> mutate(cluster = cl) |> group_by(cluster) |>
                  summarise(n = n(), across(all_of(feature_cols), ~ round(to_pct(median(.x)), 1))),
    ari       = mclust::adjustedRandIndex(features$story, cl)
  )
}

cmp <- map(c(3, 4, 5), compare_k) |> set_names(c("K3", "K4", "K5"))

# Main test: K = 5
cmp$K5$counts
cmp$K5$row_pct
cmp$K5$top_share
cmp$K5$profile      # median % growth per year in each cluster, to read what each cluster is

# Overall agreement at each K
map_dfr(cmp, \(x) tibble(ARI = round(x$ari, 2)), .id = "K")
```

**Understand:** `top_cluster_pct` is the share of a class's combos that land in its most
common cluster. 100% means the class is one cluster; low values mean the class is spread
across several. The `profile` table shows what each cluster looks like, so you can see
which class it resembles. ARI: 1 = identical groupings, 0 = no better than chance.

**Result:** _(fill in after running)_

# 8. PCA picture

k-means used 3 numbers per combo; PCA squashes them into 2 so we can draw them.

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(clust_data)   # already standardised, so no extra scaling

# How much of the information each component keeps
p_scree <- fviz_eig(pca, addlabels = TRUE) + theme_minimal()
p_scree
save_plot(p_scree, "07_pca_scree", w = 7, h = 4.5)

# Loadings: what each component "means"
round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2)
```

**Understand the loadings:** big positive or negative numbers tell you what drives each
axis. E.g. if PC1 loads strongly on the long-run window, call it "long-run growth";
if PC2 is mostly the COVID window, call it "COVID sensitivity". Name them in the report
instead of writing "Dim1 (xx%)".

```{r pca-biplot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
p_biplot <- fviz_pca_biplot(pca,
                            geom.ind = "point",
                            habillage = factor(cluster_vec),
                            addEllipses = TRUE, ellipse.type = "convex",
                            col.var = "black", repel = TRUE,
                            title = "Clusters on the first two principal components") +
  theme_minimal()
p_biplot
save_plot(p_biplot, "08_pca_biplot", w = 9, h = 7)
```

**Understand:** arrows show which direction each growth window pushes a combo. Clusters
sitting on the side an arrow points to are strong in that window.

```{r pca-labelled, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
# Same picture, but points sized by number of establishments, with the biggest labelled
pca_scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) |>
  bind_cols(features |> select(combo, mean_est)) |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster_vec))

p_pca_size <- ggplot(pca_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = mean_est), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = slice_max(pca_scores, mean_est, n = 10),
            aes(label = combo), size = 2.6, vjust = -1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Where the establishments sit",
       subtitle = "Point size = average establishments per year; 10 largest combos labelled",
       size = "Avg establishments", colour = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_pca_size
save_plot(p_pca_size, "09_pca_sized", w = 10, h = 7)
```

## 9a. Size of each cluster and its "report card"

```{r profile-table}
# Convert log changes back to approximate % per year for readability
to_pct <- function(g) (exp(g) - 1) * 100

cluster_profile <- clustered |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n_combos      = n(),
    avg_estabs    = sum(mean_est),
    across(all_of(feature_cols), ~ round(to_pct(median(.x)), 1)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_of_city_estabs = round(avg_estabs / sum(avg_estabs) * 100, 1)) |>
  relocate(pct_of_city_estabs, .after = avg_estabs)

cluster_profile
```

**Understand:** the growth columns are the **median % change per year** in each window
for combos in that cluster. `pct_of_city_estabs` tells you how much of Melbourne's
business base each cluster represents: a policy-relevant number for the report.

```{r profile-heatmap, fig.height = 4}
centroids <- clust_data |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster_vec)) |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), mean)) |>
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "feature", values_to = "z") |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature_labels[feature], levels = feature_labels))

p_centroids <- ggplot(centroids, aes(feature, cluster, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(z, 1)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = red, mid = "white", high = blue) +
  labs(title = "Cluster 'report cards'",
       subtitle = "Standardised growth vs the average combo (0 = average, +1 = 1 SD above)",
       x = NULL, y = "Cluster", fill = "SDs from\naverage") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_centroids
save_plot(p_centroids, "10_cluster_report_cards", w = 9, h = 4)
```

**Understand:** red = this cluster did worse than typical in that window, blue = better.
Read across a row to get each cluster's story (e.g. "grew fast in the long run, crashed hardest
in COVID, weak recovery").

## 9b. Year: trajectory of each cluster

```{r trajectory-total}
traj <- panel |>
  inner_join(clustered |> select(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, cluster),
             by = c("clue_small_area", "anzsic_indusrty")) |>
  group_by(cluster, year) |>
  summarise(est = sum(est), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(cluster) |>

p_traj <- ggplot(traj, aes(year, index, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(2018, 2022), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Active establishments by cluster, 2002 = 100",
       subtitle = "Dotted lines: window boundaries (2018, 2022)",
       x = "Census year", y = "Index (2002 = 100)", colour = "Cluster") +

p_traj
save_plot(p_traj, "11_cluster_trajectories")
```

**Check:** a cluster that started from a tiny 2002 base (Docklands-heavy) will shoot up
on this index. If so, the next plot is the fairer comparison.

```{r trajectory-spaghetti, fig.height = 7}
# Each combo's line relative to its own 2002–24 average, plus the cluster median in bold
traj_combo <- panel |>
  inner_join(clustered |> select(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, cluster, mean_est, combo),
             by = c("clue_small_area", "anzsic_indusrty")) |>
  mutate(rel = est / mean_est * 100)

traj_median <- traj_combo |>
  group_by(cluster, year) |>
  summarise(rel = median(rel), .groups = "drop")

p_spaghetti <- ggplot(traj_combo, aes(year, rel)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(2018, 2022), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(group = combo), colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = traj_median, colour = red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster, labeller = label_both) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(title = "Every combo's path, grouped by cluster",
       subtitle = "Grey = one area-industry combo; red = cluster median; dotted = window boundaries (2018, 2022). 100 = that combo's 2002–24 average",
       x = "Census year", y = "Establishments (% of own average)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
p_spaghetti
save_plot(p_spaghetti, "12_cluster_spaghetti", w = 10, h = 7)
```

**Check:** grey lines within a panel should roughly follow the red line. If a panel's
grey lines go in all directions, that cluster isn't a clean segment.

## 9c. Industry and area: the full map

```{r grid-map, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 8}
grid <- features_all |>
  select(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, mean_est) |>
  left_join(clustered |> select(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, cluster),
            by = c("clue_small_area", "anzsic_indusrty")) |>
  mutate(cluster = fct_na_value_to_level(cluster, level = "Too small"))

p_grid <- ggplot(grid, aes(clue_small_area, anzsic_indusrty, fill = cluster)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(mean_est >= MIN_EST, round(mean_est), "")), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(setNames(scales::hue_pal()(K), 1:K), "Too small" = grey)) +
  labs(title = "Which cluster each industry-in-an-area belongs to",
       subtitle = paste0("Number = average active establishments per year; grey = fewer than ",
                         MIN_EST, " per year (not clustered)"),
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
p_grid
save_plot(p_grid, "13_area_industry_grid", w = 11, h = 8)
```

**Understand:** this is probably your single most useful exhibit.

- A **row mostly one colour** means that industry behaves the same everywhere: an
  industry-wide story.
- A **column mostly one colour** means that area drags all its industries along: an
  area story.
- A **patchwork** means it depends on the specific combination, which is the insight
  the separate area and industry analyses couldn't show.

# Stability tests

```{r}
run_km <- function(feat, k = K, cols = feature_cols) {
  set.seed(123)
  setNames(kmeans(scale(feat[, cols]), k, nstart = 50)$cluster, feat$combo)
}
compare_to_base <- function(new) {
  base <- setNames(cluster_vec, features$combo)
  shared <- intersect(names(base), names(new))
  mclust::adjustedRandIndex(base[shared], new[shared])
}

# (a) Size threshold: does dropping more or fewer tiny combos change things?
map_dfr(c(5, 15, 20), \(m) tibble(
  MIN_EST = m, n_combos = sum(features_all$mean_est >= m),
  ARI = compare_to_base(run_km(filter(features_all, mean_est >= m)))))

# (b) Time windows: shift the endpoints a year (also helps with the carried-forward years)
features_shift <- features |> mutate(
  g_long     = ann_log_change(y2002, y2019, 17),
  g_covid    = ann_log_change(y2019, y2022, 3),
  g_recovery = ann_log_change(y2022, y2024, 2))
compare_to_base(run_km(features_shift))

# (c) Drop one window at a time: does any single period decide everything?
map_dfr(feature_cols, \(f) tibble(
  dropped = f, ARI = compare_to_base(run_km(features, cols = setdiff(feature_cols, f)))))

# (d) Outliers: re-run without Docklands
compare_to_base(run_km(filter(features, clue_small_area != "Docklands")))

# (e) Neighbouring K: how do the clusters split or merge at K = 3 and 5?
table(K4 = cluster_vec, K3 = run_km(features, k = 3))
table(K4 = cluster_vec, K5 = run_km(features, k = 5))

hc <- hclust(dist(clust_data), method = "ward.D2")
mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster_vec, cutree(hc, K))

table(kmeans = cluster_vec, ward = cutree(hc, K))
table(kmeans = cluster_vec, pam = pam_fit$clustering)

base <- setNames(cluster_vec, features$combo)

runs <- list(
  base         = base,
  min5         = run_km(filter(features_all, mean_est >= 5)),
  min15        = run_km(filter(features_all, mean_est >= 15)),
  min20        = run_km(filter(features_all, mean_est >= 20)),
  windows      = run_km(features_shift),
  no_docklands = run_km(filter(features, clue_small_area != "Docklands")),
  K3           = run_km(features, k = 3),
  K5           = run_km(features, k = 5),
  pam          = setNames(pam_fit$clustering, features$combo),
  ward         = setNames(cutree(hc, K), features$combo)
)

# In each run, find the cluster holding most of our cluster-1 combos, and flag its members.
# Assumes cluster 1 (weakest overall growth) is the decliner group: confirm on the three-window fit.
flag_decliners <- function(new) {
  b1 <- intersect(names(base)[base == 1], names(new))
  target <- as.integer(names(which.max(table(new[b1]))))
  new == target
}

consensus <- map(runs, flag_decliners) |>
  map(\(x) enframe(x, "combo", "flagged")) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "run") |>
  group_by(combo) |>
  summarise(n_runs = n(), n_flagged = sum(flagged), pct_flagged = n_flagged / n_runs) |>
  filter(n_flagged > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_flagged), desc(n_flagged))

consensus |> print(n = 40)
```
